transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-09
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 56 minutes (recording)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Lumos CTO), Sara Mehta (Lumos ML Eng), Tom Ruiz (Lumos Infra)

[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round of intros? I'm Avery, AE on the Redwood side. Marcus and Priya are my SEs.
[00:14] Daniel Park: Hi, Daniel here, CTO at Lumos. Quick note, we're trying to scope a POC to understand both performance and the actual economics — per token, per request, the whole thing.
[00:28] Sara Mehta: Sara, ML eng. We'll be running a retrieval-augmented generation workflow, mostly short prompts with long-ish knowledge context.
[00:36] Tom Ruiz: Tom, infra. I care about networking, VPC peering, and what telemetry you'll need.
[00:41] Marcus Lee: Great, glad to hear. High-level agenda: success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, cost modeling assumptions, and timelines. Sound good?
[00:48] Daniel: Yeah. We'll start with the success criteria. For us it's: accuracy comparable to our current model baseline, p95 latency under 300ms for the trimmed user path, and cost under $X/month — which I know is vague — but think of an upper bound of $5k/month for the pilot.
[01:05] Avery: Perfect. Can you clarify what you mean by "trimmed user path"?
[01:10] Sara: The path that hits the assistant with a single retrieval result, so 1 RAG hit and the generation of ~250 tokens. So roughly 250-400 tokens per call when you include prompt + context + response.
[01:22] Marcus: That's super helpful. We'll model for a median of 300 tokens per request and a 95th percentile of 900 tokens for heavier cases.
[01:31] Priya Nair: Also want to call out the importance of caching — prefix caching and KV cache for repeated contexts can drop unit costs dramatically, so we'll test with and without those enabled.
[01:44] Tom: How much of an impact are we talking? When does it make sense to use dedicated capacity vs hosted?
[01:51] Marcus: Ballpark: good batching + prefix caching can reduce per-token inferred compute by 30-60% depending on repetition. For dedicated reserved pools, you get better sustained throughput and lower per-token cost at scale because of amortized GPU utilization. Hosted is simpler for a short POC but might be more expensive per token.
[02:07] Daniel: Okay. For budget reasons we might need to limit test volume. We can do 100k calls over 2 weeks as a start. Does that give you enough signal?
[02:16] Avery: Yes, 100k calls at median 300 tokens gives us 30M tokens — adequate to model economics. We'll also run a smaller high-latency tail test to capture p95/p99.
[02:27] Sara: We want to understand cost per million tokens in different configurations: no batching, conservative batching, aggressive batching, with and without KV/prefix cache. Also quantized vs fp16.
[02:40] Marcus: We'll include those in the spreadsheet. Typical CR numbers we surface: hosted baseline might be around $12-$30 per million tokens depending on model size and infra; dedicated reserved can drop to $4-$12 per million at sufficient utilization; private on-prem with quantization can go lower but depends on infra and ops. These are ballpark figures and we'll run real benchmarks to refine.
[03:02] Daniel: That spread is big. We'll need hard numbers for our dataset.
[03:07] Priya: We'll design a benchmark matrix: axes are model variant (small/medium/large), batching policy (none/auto/aggressive), caching (off/prefix/KV), quantization (fp16/8-bit), and traffic pattern (synthetic uniform vs production replay). For each cell we'll capture tokens, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, and cost estimate.
[03:26] Tom: For the POC we'll be running inside our VPC if we go private; but for speed we'll accept hosted initially. Are there any telemetry or logs we can't get on hosted?
[03:36] Marcus: On hosted we provide token-level cost breakdowns, per-request latency and traces, and model-level throughput. For private we'll add full access to metrics and you can hook up your own Prometheus. We cannot provide raw PII from other tenants; but you can stream anonymized traces.
[03:49] Daniel: Security checklist — we'll need SOC2, SAML SSO, and KMS support. Priya will share the security pack?
[03:55] Priya: Yep, I'll send SOC2 and our encryption-at-rest docs after the call.
[03:59] Sara: Back to economics — is there a formula you usually share? Like per-request cost = token_count * per_token_rate + overhead?
[04:07] Avery: Yes, that's the simple model. Then we layer in amortized GPU infra, reserved discounts, and additional ops overhead. We'll provide three scenarios: (A) hosted pay-as-you-go with default batching, (B) dedicated reserved with target utilization at 60%-80%, (C) private on-prem assuming quantized model and 75% utilization.
[04:23] Daniel: For (B) what utilization do you need to hit the lower per-token?
[04:28] Marcus: Typically >50% sustained GPU utilization on inference server-level; if you can push 70-80% that's when unit economics look the best. That depends on request concurrency and batching policy.
[04:38] Tom: Concurrency — our frontend is going to send bursts. How do you account for burst capacity?
[04:43] Priya: We support burst pools and autoscaling for Dedicated. For hosted we'll configure a routing policy to use fallback model variants if capacity is constrained to avoid errors. That affects quality but keeps availability.
[04:55] Sara: For benchmark plan, we want to measure token-level cost and quality delta vs our ground truth for 3 models. Can we include a reranking pass as part of the flow?
[05:04] Marcus: Yes, include reranking. We'll instrument the pipeline so reranker calls and generation calls are counted separately; that helps show where tokens are spent.
[05:12] Daniel: Timeline — we want a 6-week pilot. Week 1: finalize scope and samples; Week 2: baseline runs; Weeks 3-4: variant tests and cache/batching experiments; Week 5: integration checks with VPC; Week 6: results and decision.
[05:29] Avery: That timeline is reasonable. We'll aim to have cost spreadsheet and benchmark plan within 2 business days.
[05:35] Sara: On the data side, some prompts have PII in them — we'll scrub before sending. Any constraints on synthetic vs real data?
[05:43] Priya: Prefer real-ish data for quality signal but scrubbed is fine. We can also run a synthetic replay if needed to preserve privacy and still get utilization metrics.
[05:52] Tom: Network egress costs — when we talk about per-token cost, do you include cloud egress or is that separate?
[05:58] Marcus: We typically exclude customer-side egress; our per-token covers compute and infra. If you route through Redwood-managed connectors with storage, we'll call that out separately.
[06:07] Daniel: Ok. For the benchmark, what tooling do you use so we can reproduce?
[06:11] Marcus: We use a reproducible benchmark harness (we'll share) that can replay logs, simulate concurrency, and collect traces. It outputs a CSV with tokens, latencies, GPU metrics, and estimated cost per million tokens per cell. We'll share the harness repo link.
[06:23] Sara: Will you be running with different sequence lengths? We have a long tail of 2k tokens for some internal flows.
[06:29] Priya: Yes we'll include sequence length buckets: short (<512), medium (512-1024), long (1024-2048). We'll compute weighted averages based on your sample distribution.
[06:38] Daniel: For quality success, what's acceptable? 95% of responses must have similarity > 0.8 to our golden set?
[06:44] Avery: We can accept a similarity metric as a success criterion. We'll propose thresholds: top-line quality parity (>=0.85 on your metric) for at least 90% of queries and no regression in critical categories. But final thresholds are customer-defined.
[06:58] Sara: I want to see the cost delta when enabling prefix caching. In our workload a lot of queries reuse the same context.
[07:05] Marcus: We'll run experiments that hold everything constant and flip cache on/off. Expect prefix cache to reduce token generation by deduplicating repeated context tokens, often reducing effective compute by 20-40% in RAG-heavy flows.
[07:18] Tom: Regarding quantization, do you need SRE support to run int8 models or can we do that in hosted?
[07:25] Priya: We can run quantized variants on both hosted and private. Hosted supports our common 8-bit workflows; for on-prem we help with compilation and kernel selection. But ops burden is higher in private.
[07:36] Daniel: Pricing for quantized models — are they cheaper per token only because of lower GPU utilization?
[07:42] Marcus: Right, quantization reduces memory and compute, enabling smaller instance types or greater throughput; savings show up in lower amortized GPU cost per token. But we need benchmarks because quality delta can exist.
[07:53] Sara: I also want to measure developer velocity impact — i.e., how many iterations to get rollout-ready. Can we include a small integration checklist?
[08:01] Avery: Yes, we'll include an integration checklist: API keys, SSO, VPC peering steps, sample code, and model pinning instructions for rollouts.
[08:10] Daniel: Any gotchas you usually see in POCs like ours?
[08:14] Marcus: Common issues: mismatched tokenization assumptions between eval harness and production, overfitting to synthetic prompts, and not accounting for tail latency in the cost model. We'll enumerate those in the benchmark doc.
[08:26] Tom: On telemetry, can we get per-customer traces and sample payloads for debug?
[08:31] Priya: Yes for private; on hosted we provide anonymized traces and token-level timing breakdowns. We can also run a debug window where you share sanitized sample payloads in a secure channel.
[08:42] Sara: Regarding fallback policies you mentioned — can we define quality thresholds to trigger model fallback?
[08:47] Marcus: Yes. Example policy: if p95 latency > 500ms for 3 contiguous 5-min windows, route to a smaller model variant for new requests while allowing existing in-flight requests to finish. That keeps availability while preserving best-effort quality.
[09:01] Daniel: If we need to reduce cost mid-pilot, can you throttle or switch to a cheaper model automatically?
[09:07] Avery: Yes, routing and autoscaling policies let you prioritize cost vs latency. We'll show a few tradeoff knobs in the spreadsheet.
[09:14] Sara: For the cost model spreadsheet, can you show a sample calculation now?
[09:18] Marcus: Briefly: cost_per_request = (prompt_tokens + response_tokens) * per_token_rate + compute_overhead. Per_token_rate is derived from GPU hourly cost / effective tokens per hour. So if a GPU costs $X/hr and processes Y tokens/hr under a given batching policy, per_token_rate = X/Y. Then add service margin.
[09:35] Daniel: For our 30M-token test, can you give a rough total cost estimate across those three scenarios?
[09:41] Marcus: Rough rough: hosted baseline maybe $350-$900 for 30M tokens depending on model; dedicated reserved could be $120-$360 if utilization is good; private varies widely but might be in same ballpark or lower after ops. We'll put exact cells in spreadsheet.
[09:58] Sara: That helps. We'll need to check the CPU/GPU mix when you run the benchmark.
[10:03] Marcus: We'll report GPU utilization, GPU memory, CPU load, and any observed stalls due to data loading.
[10:10] Tom: If we do a VPC peering test in week 5, what do you need from our side?
[10:15] Priya: VPC details, firewall rules, and a test account. We'll provide a template and exact ports.
[10:21] Daniel: Ok. Any objections or constraints from your side on timeline?
[10:25] Avery: Nothing major. We might need a two-day lead to provision some dedicated capacity if you want reserved trial GPUs.
[10:31] Sara: Let's plan for that if numbers look good after baseline.
[10:35] Marcus: One more thing: we'll run two types of benchmarks — synthetic uniform concurrency to exercise throughput, and production-replay for quality and realistic tail latency. Both are important for unit economics.
[10:47] Daniel: Agreed. Let's talk about acceptance criteria one more time.
[10:51] Avery: Acceptance criteria draft: 1) Quality parity >=0.85 on your metric for >=90% of samples; 2) p95 latency <= 300ms for the trimmed path; 3) Cost estimate for scaled deployment is within 20% of pilot model or you have a committed plan to reach target via batching/quantization; 4) Integration checklist completed with no major blockers.
[11:14] Sara: Looks good. If we fail one, do we get additional time to iterate?
[11:18] Avery: Yes, typically we budget an iteration cycle for an additional 2 weeks to tune batching and caching.
[11:24] Tom: About the iteration, who drives changes on your side?
[11:28] Marcus: SEs (Priya and Marcus) will lead the tuning; Avery coordinates product and commercial conversations. We'll set times for weekly syncs.
[11:37] Daniel: Great. Last question: can you include an explicit per-request example in the spreadsheet so we can map to our billing lines?
[11:43] Avery: Absolutely. We'll include a sample calculation row that maps token counts to per-token rates to subtotal and then show a monthly extrapolation.
[11:50] Sara: Perfect. Anything else?
[11:52] Priya: I'll upload the SOC2 and KMS docs, Marcus will post the benchmark harness link, and Avery will send the cost spreadsheet.
[12:00] Daniel: Thanks, all. We'll aim to have sample prompts ready by next Monday.
[12:05] Avery: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the baseline run.
[12:10] End of recording.
